topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Decimals
topic.scope: place value of decimals, comparing decimals, decimals and fractions, operations on decimals, money and measurement

nodes.name: Operations on Decimals
external_prereqs: addition and subtraction of whole numbers

misconceptions.statement: The decimal point separates two independent whole numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students see the numbers to the left and right as separate entities rather than a single value.
misconceptions.fix: The decimal point is a marker that indicates the start of fractional parts (tenths, hundredths) smaller than one.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: A decimal with more digits is always larger.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the whole number rule where more digits mean a larger magnitude.
misconceptions.fix: Compare digits from left to right starting at the highest place value; 0.5 is larger than 0.12.
misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: To add decimals, align the last digits on the right.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the rule for adding whole numbers where the rightmost column is always the units.
misconceptions.fix: Always align the decimal points to ensure that tenths are added to tenths and hundredths to hundredths.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The tenths place is the first place to the right of the decimal, so it represents the smallest value.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the order of fractional parts with whole number place values.
misconceptions.fix: The tenths place is larger than the hundredths place because 1/10 is greater than 1/100.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: 0.5 is smaller than 0.05 because 5 is the same in both and 0.05 has an extra zero, so it is bigger.
misconceptions.why: Student treats zeros after the point as adding value, like trailing zeros making a whole number bigger, and ignores place value.
misconceptions.fix: Compare digit by digit from the left: 0.5 has 5 tenths while 0.05 has 0 tenths and 5 hundredths. So 0.5 > 0.05 (0.5 = 0.50 = 50 hundredths).
misconceptions.root_belief: Zeros after the point increase a number's size

misconceptions.statement: A decimal with fewer digits is always larger, so 0.8 is larger than 0.83.
misconceptions.why: Student over-corrects the 'longer is larger' idea and links hundredths to smallness, believing the shorter decimal is bigger, as with 1/8 vs 1/83 denominators.
misconceptions.fix: Write both with the same number of places: 0.8 = 0.80, and 0.83 > 0.80. Compare place by place after equalising digits.
misconceptions.root_belief: Fewer digits after point means larger value
misconceptions.source_hint: research on decimal comparison (e.g. Resnick, Stacey & Steinle)

misconceptions.statement: 0.4 and 0.40 are different numbers, and 0.40 is greater.
misconceptions.why: Student believes extra digits change the quantity and does not see that a trailing zero shows only a finer subdivision of the same length.
misconceptions.fix: Show 0.4 and 0.40 on the same number line or 10x10 grid: 4 tenths = 40 hundredths, the same point. Trailing zeros after the last digit do not change the value.

probe.question: Is 0.4 equal to 0.40? If not, which is greater?

misconceptions.root_belief: Trailing zeros after the point change value

misconceptions.statement: 0.25 as a fraction is 1/25 (or 25/10), because you just move the digits over the fraction bar.
misconceptions.why: Student copies the digits without linking the number of decimal places to the power of ten in the denominator.
misconceptions.fix: The denominator is 10, 100, 1000 as per the number of decimal places. 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4. Read it as 'twenty-five hundredths'.
misconceptions.root_belief: Fraction denominator is just the decimal digits

misconceptions.statement: 0.3 is the same as 1/3 because both have a 3.
misconceptions.why: Student matches digits across notations without realising a decimal digit in tenths means 3 out of 10 equal parts.
misconceptions.fix: 0.3 = 3/10 (three tenths), but 1/3 is one of three equal parts, about 0.333.... They are different numbers.

probe.question: Is 0.3 equal to 1/3? Give a reason.

misconceptions.root_belief: Same digit in different notation means same value

misconceptions.statement: The hundredths place is the second place after the decimal and 0.07 means 7 tenths.
misconceptions.why: Student reads the digit by the number of places or by its digit and ignores which place it sits in, so zero in the tenths place is skipped.
misconceptions.fix: 0.07: tenths digit is 0, hundredths digit is 7, so it means 7 hundredths = 7/100. Place holders (zeros) keep digits in the correct position.

probe.question: What is the value of the 7 in 0.07?

misconceptions.root_belief: Zero placeholders can be ignored when reading value

misconceptions.statement: When adding a whole number to a decimal, the whole number needs no decimal point, so 5 + 0.3 = 0.8 (digits just line up).
misconceptions.why: Student treats the whole number as having no point and aligns digits to the right or adds 5 and 3 as digits, ignoring that 5 is 5.0 with the point at its right end.
misconceptions.fix: Write 5 as 5.0 so decimal points are in a line: 5.0 + 0.3 = 5.3. A whole number has an invisible point after its ones digit.
misconceptions.root_belief: Whole numbers have no decimal point to align

misconceptions.statement: When subtracting decimals, you can take the smaller digit from the larger one in each place, so 5.2 - 1.7 = 4.5.
misconceptions.why: Student applies 'always larger minus smaller' per column without regrouping across the decimal point, as in whole-number column errors.
misconceptions.fix: Align points and regroup: 5.2 = 4 ones + 12 tenths, so 12 - 7 = 5 tenths and 4 - 1 = 3 ones; the answer is 3.5. Check by adding 3.5 + 1.7 = 5.2.
misconceptions.root_belief: Subtract smaller from larger digit in each column
